Black-chinned hummingbird (Archilochus alexandri) eggs, incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], typically hatch after 15 days [ab = 15 days], a developmental period derived from the mean of several measurements. At the moment of hatching, neonates emerge at a total length of 0.64 centimeters [Lb = 0.64 centimeters], a value that reflects the constraints imposed by the calcareous eggshell. Newly hatched chicks weigh only 0.33 grams [Wwb = 0.33 grams] upon emergence, an exceedingly small mass that is characteristic of altricial hummingbird nestlings requiring intensive parental brooding and frequent provisioning. This minimal starting size necessitates a period of rapid somatic growth during the early nestling phase, during which the downy chick is entirely dependent on the female for warmth and the male for territorial defense.

Under the thermal conditions approximating active metabolic heat production (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), the young fledge at 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching], a mean value obtained from repeated field observations. The first successful brood, however, is not initiated until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], indicating a substantial delay between physiological sexual maturation and the actual commencement of breeding activity at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This lag likely arises from the need to acquire a territory, establish a dominance hierarchy, and accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support the extraordinary energetic demands of egg production and nesting.

A sample of 95 adults yielded a mean ultimate wet weight of 4.16 grams [Wwi = 4.16 grams], a value that represents the maximum recorded body mass in this species. The ultimate length, attained by fully grown breeding individuals, is 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters] from the tip of the bill to the end of the tail feathers. These morphological endpoints, combined with the very low hatchling mass, illustrate the steep growth trajectory required to achieve adult dimensions. The reproductive strategy built upon this developmental foundation is relatively conservative. Each breeding season, a female typically initiates just two clutches [F_R_i = breeding season, a female typically initiates just two clutches], a rate constrained by the time required for incubation and the subsequent provisioning of the altricial young.

The lifespan of Archilochus alexandri is notable for its brevity relative to many other birds of similar body size. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild is 3960 days [am = 3960 days] at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a figure derived from banding recapture data. This corresponds to nearly 11 years, though most individuals likely survive only a single or a few breeding seasons due to high rates of predation and the metabolic toll of migration. The species undertakes extensive seasonal movements between breeding grounds in western North America and wintering sites in Mexico, a journey that imposes substantial energetic costs and elevates mortality risk. During the breeding season, males establish feeding territories that they defend vigorously; the successful acquisition of a high-quality territory with abundant nectar sources is a critical determinant of reproductive success and, ultimately, survival.

Comparatively, the life-history parameters of the Black-chinned hummingbird align closely with those of its congener, Archilochus colubris, although subtle differences in body size and migratory distance produce minor variation in developmental timing. The natural mortality experienced by this species is heavily concentrated during the post-fledging dispersal phase and the initial migration southward. Annual adult survival estimates remain poorly resolved but are presumed to be moderate for a bird of this metabolic capacity. Future research focusing on the energetic costs of torpor use during cold nights may clarify how individuals manage to persist for 3960 days [am = 3960 days] under the demanding conditions of their environment at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Understanding these physiological trade-offs is essential for predicting population responses to ongoing habitat alteration and climate change across the species' extensive geographic range.
